clean_source_blocks.text: Landmark finding against supermarket giant after competition watchdog argued discounts did not represent genuine savings Coles misled Australian shoppers with fake discounts on everyday grocery products, the federal court has ruled in a landmark decision for the supermarket industry. Justice Michael O’Bryan handed down his judgment on Thursday, delivering a significant blow to Australia’s second largest supermarket chain, which had argued the discounts represented genuine savings during a period of high inflation. Continue reading...

Landmark finding against supermarket giant after competition watchdog argued discounts did not represent genuine savings Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast Coles misled Australian shoppers with fake discounts on everyday grocery products, the federal court has ruled in a landmark decision for the supermarket industry. Justice Michael O’Bryan handed down his judgment on Thursday, delivering a significant blow to Australia’s second-largest supermarket chain, which had argued the discounts represented genuine savings during a period of high inflation. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) sued Coles and rival Woolworths, accusing the supermarket giants of duping shoppers by using promotional programs to disguise price increases on hundreds of products.

During its trial in February, Coles conceded that by the time it raised the price of an item from the original to the “was” price, the supermarket had already planned and agreed with the supplier on what the new “Down Down” price would be. Legal counsel for the supermarket, however, argued that the promotional prices were genuine discounts offered to shoppers after an increase in wholesale costs charged by suppliers during a period of rising inflation. Reading a summary of his judgment in a Melbourne court room on Thursday, O’Bryan agreed the price increases were done in “ordinary commercial way” and Coles had been meeting requests from suppliers. However, the judge upheld the ACCC’s allegation that Coles falsely promoted “discounts” on these products based on increased prices that had been available for too short a period.

The outcome of two cases against Woolworths and Coles will ultimately reveal whether supermarket shoppers were duped by promotional prices. (ABC News: Billy Cooper) You can imagine the alarm bells going off for Paul Harker as he browsed the colourful aisles of his local Woolworths. The senior Woolworths' executive was searching for the bright red Prices Dropped tickets that promise long-term savings on household staples. But Harker wasn't looking for a bargain — he was trying to work out if the supermarket giant had a serious problem. Mid-way through 2022, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) had come knocking, probing its prominent discounting program. That would eventually result in the bombshell lawsuit Woolies now faces in which it is accused of misleading shoppers with fake discounts on more than 260 items — something it denies.

[Lähde: The Guardian World]
Landmark finding against supermarket giant after competition watchdog argued discounts did not represent genuine savings

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Coles misled Australian shoppers with fake discounts on everyday grocery products, the federal court has ruled in a landmark decision for the supermarket industry.

Justice Michael O’Bryan handed down his judgment on Thursday, delivering a significant blow to Australia’s second-largest supermarket chain, which had argued the discounts represented genuine savings during a period of high inflation.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) sued Coles and rival Woolworths, accusing the supermarket giants of duping shoppers by using promotional programs to disguise price increases on hundreds of products.

In the Coles case, the supermarket sold 245 products at one price for a median period of a year, before being increased to a second price, for a median of just 28 days, before reducing them to a third price which was more expensive or equal to the first price.

The strategy is known as “was/is” comparative pricing: Coles advertised products to shoppers with “Down Down” promotional tickets that displayed their new, supposedly discounted “is” price next to the higher “was” price.

But the supermarket did not disclose on the tickets that the “was” prices had been in place for only a short period and that the items were sold at a cheaper price before that.

During its trial in February, Coles conceded that by the time it raised the price of an item from the original to the “was” price, the supermarket had already planned and agreed with the supplier on what the new “Down Down” price would be.

Legal counsel for the supermarket, however, argued that the promotional prices were genuine discounts offered to shoppers after an increase in wholesale costs charged by suppliers during a period of rising inflation.

Reading a summary of his judgment in a Melbourne court room on Thursday, O’Bryan agreed the price increases were done in “ordinary commercial way” and Coles had been meeting requests from suppliers.

However, the judge upheld the ACCC’s allegation that Coles falsely promoted “discounts” on these products based on increased prices that had been available for too short a period.

O’Bryan said if the average shopper had known the “was” prices on the items’ promotional tickets had been in place for such a short 

---

[Lähde: ABC (Australian Broadcasting Corporation)]
The outcome of two cases against Woolworths and Coles will ultimately reveal whether supermarket shoppers were duped by promotional prices. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

You can imagine the alarm bells going off for Paul Harker as he browsed the colourful aisles of his local Woolworths.

The senior Woolworths' executive was searching for the bright red Prices Dropped tickets that promise long-term savings on household staples.

But Harker wasn't looking for a bargain — he was trying to work out if the supermarket giant had a serious problem.

Mid-way through 2022, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) had come knocking, probing its prominent discounting program.

That would eventually result in the bombshell lawsuit Woolies now faces in which it is accused of misleading shoppers with fake discounts on more than 260 items — something it denies.

It was in the laundry aisle that Harker spotted his first problem.

The Prices Dropped ticket for a Fab Laundry powder offered a huge saving — down from a higher "was" price of $14 to just $8.

Harker immediately realised the $14 "was" price tag was "too high" compared to the discounted price.

He yanked the Fab powder from the Prices Dropped program, later finding out the $14 price tag was the supplier's proposed recommended retail price.

The federal court case against Woolies is expected to wrap up this week and another remarkably similar one against Coles is awaiting judgment.

The outcome of both cases will ultimately reveal whether supermarket shoppers have been screwed over with dubious discounts.

Both cases against the major supermarkets have the potential to reshape retail pricing. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

During the proceedings, the focus has been on trying to establish whether grocery items were given genuine reductions.

This meant items needed to have a higher previous "was" price for long enough to ensure it was considered legitimate.

But the problem is there has been no clear red line that states how long that period should be and experts say picking one is highly problematic.

That left Woolies and Coles to make educated guesses about where the red line should be by writing their own internal guidelines.

What both cases exposed was how those policies clashed with the profit motive driving two of Australia's biggest retailers.

payload.title: Australialainen oikeus katsoi Colesin johtaneen asiakkaita harhaan alennuskampanjalla
payload.summary: Australian liittovaltion tuomioistuin on katsonut, että supermarketketju Coles johti asiakkaita harhaan Down Down -alennuskampanjallaan. Ratkaisu koskee arjen elintarvikkeiden hinnoittelua ja alennusväitteitä.
payload.content:
Australian liittovaltion tuomioistuin on katsonut, että maan toiseksi suurin supermarketketju Coles johti asiakkaita harhaan Down Down -alennuskampanjallaan, jossa arjen ruokatuotteita markkinoitiin alennettuina. Tuomari Michael O’Bryan antoi ratkaisunsa torstaina Melbournessa. Päätös on merkittävä Australian vähittäiskaupalle, sillä kilpailuviranomainen oli väittänyt, etteivät kampanjassa esitetyt säästöt olleet todellisia.

## Kiista koski alennusten aitoutta

Australian kilpailu- ja kuluttajaviranomainen ACCC haastoi Colesin oikeuteen ja syytti yhtiötä siitä, että se käytti kampanjoita peittääkseen hinnankorotuksia sadoissa tuotteissa. Viranomaisen mukaan asiakkaille annettiin harhaanjohtava kuva siitä, että he saisivat aidon alennuksen aiempaan hintaan verrattuna.

Oikeudenkäynnissä Coles myönsi, että kun tuotteen hinta nostettiin alkuperäisestä hinnasta niin sanotuksi vertailuhinnaksi, yhtiö oli jo suunnitellut ja sopinut tavarantoimittajan kanssa uudesta Down Down -kampanjahinnasta. Tämä oli keskeistä viranomaisen väitteelle: alennusta verrattiin hintaan, joka oli ollut voimassa vain lyhyen ajan.

Coles puolusti menettelyään sillä, että kampanjahinnat olivat todellisia alennuksia tilanteessa, jossa tavarantoimittajien tukkuhinnat olivat nousseet inflaation aikana. Yhtiön mukaan hinnankorotukset johtuivat kaupallisista syistä eivätkä olleet keinotekoinen tapa luoda harhaanjohtavia alennuksia.

## Tuomari hyväksyi osan selityksestä, mutta piti markkinointia harhaanjohtavana

Tuomari O’Bryan hyväksyi sen, että hinnankorotukset oli tehty tavanomaisessa kaupallisessa prosessissa ja että Coles oli reagoinut tavarantoimittajien pyyntöihin. Hän kuitenkin hyväksyi kilpailuviranomaisen keskeisen väitteen siitä, että Coles markkinoi alennuksia harhaanjohtavasti, koska vertailuhinnat olivat olleet käytössä liian lyhyen aikaa.

Ratkaisu on takaisku Colesille, joka on Australian toiseksi suurin supermarketketju. Tapauksen merkitystä lisää se, että ACCC on kohdistanut vastaavia väitteitä myös kilpailija Woolworthsiin. Woolworthsia koskevassa asiassa viranomainen on väittänyt, että sen alennusohjelma johti kuluttajia harhaan yli 260 tuotteen kohdalla; yhtiö on kiistänyt väitteet.

Päätös korostaa, kuinka tarkasti alennusmarkkinointia arvioidaan tilanteessa, jossa ruoan hinnat ja elinkustannukset ovat olleet kuluttajille erityisen näkyvä huolenaihe. Oikeuden linjaus voi vaikuttaa siihen, miten suuret vähittäiskauppaketjut Australiassa jatkossa esittävät kampanjahintoja ja säästöväitteitä asiakkailleen.

Kilpailuviranomainen ACCC:n mukaan alennuksia verrattiin hintoihin, jotka olivat olleet voimassa liian lyhyen ajan.
Coles perusteli hinnoitteluaan inflaatiolla ja tavarantoimittajien tukkuhintojen nousulla.

Landmark finding against supermarket giant after competition watchdog argued discounts did not represent genuine savings Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast Coles misled Australian shoppers with fake discounts on everyday grocery products, the federal court has ruled in a landmark decision for the supermarket industry. Justice Michael O’Bryan handed down his judgment on Thursday, delivering a significant blow to Australia’s second-largest supermarket chain, which had argued the discounts represented genuine savings during a period of high inflation. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) sued Coles and rival Woolworths, accusing the supermarket giants of duping shoppers by using promotional programs to disguise price increases on hundreds of products.

During its trial in February, Coles conceded that by the time it raised the price of an item from the original to the “was” price, the supermarket had already planned and agreed with the supplier on what the new “Down Down” price would be. Legal counsel for the supermarket, however, argued that the promotional prices were genuine discounts offered to shoppers after an increase in wholesale costs charged by suppliers during a period of rising inflation. Reading a summary of his judgment in a Melbourne court room on Thursday, O’Bryan agreed the price increases were done in “ordinary commercial way” and Coles had been meeting requests from suppliers. However, the judge upheld the ACCC’s allegation that Coles falsely promoted “discounts” on these products based on increased prices that had been available for too short a period.

The outcome of two cases against Woolworths and Coles will ultimately reveal whether supermarket shoppers were duped by promotional prices. (ABC News: Billy Cooper) You can imagine the alarm bells going off for Paul Harker as he browsed the colourful aisles of his local Woolworths. The senior Woolworths' executive was searching for the bright red Prices Dropped tickets that promise long-term savings on household staples. But Harker wasn't looking for a bargain — he was trying to work out if the supermarket giant had a serious problem. Mid-way through 2022, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) had come knocking, probing its prominent discounting program. That would eventually result in the bombshell lawsuit Woolies now faces in which it is accused of misleading shoppers with fake discounts on more than 260 items — something it denies.
